text: Individual EEG effect estimates and approximate confidence intervals were checked against available source statistics. Positive effects indicated an increase in the measured EEG feature associated with improved cognition, not necessarily cognitive improvement. Calculations accounted for the distinction between paired and independent-group designs where the required information was available, and digitized values were examined under alternative group allocations. Effects with unresolved design or test-statistic conflicts were excluded from numerical summaries; estimates that could not be independently reconstructed were identified as provisional. No pooled EEG effect, heterogeneity, moderator or funnel analysis was estimated. EEG–cognition associations were described separately from intervention effects.

text: Across 17 cohorts, memory and global cognition had positive pooled estimates (g = 0.281 and 0.399, respectively), but their confidence intervals included zero, leaving the evidence for benefit inconclusive. Executive function/sustained attention showed a positive pooled estimate based on three cohorts. The positive secondary overall estimate was qualified by divergent reporting-bias sensitivities. EEG findings were too heterogeneous for pooling and did not establish a validated marker of cognitive benefit. However, their narrative synthesis provides a basis for selecting candidate measures, identifying gaps in concurrent EEG and cognitive assessment, and designing studies of individualized, adaptive tPBM. Future trials should test whether within-person EEG responses predict cognitive improvement and whether using those responses to adjust stimulation improves outcomes compared with a fixed protocol.
